hints: Remember what $\text{NH}_3(\text{aq})$ really does in water, it acts as a weak base that supplies $\text{OH}^-$ ions for precipitation.
Check which metal hydroxides are insoluble, $\text{Mg}(\text{OH})_2$ is a white insoluble solid while $\text{NaOH}$ and $\text{Ba}(\text{OH})_2$ are soluble.
Consider the special behaviour of $\text{SiCl}_4(\text{l})$, a covalent chloride of Period 3 that hydrolyses completely to give white solid silica.
walkthrough:
**See what ammonia does in water**

Think of $\text{NH}_3(\text{aq})$ as a source of hydroxide ions, not just ammonia molecules. It is a weak base:

$$\text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{NH}_4^+ + \text{OH}^-$$

So the test is really, does the cation give an insoluble hydroxide with $\text{OH}^-$?

**Test the three ionic chlorides**

$\text{NaCl}$, $\text{MgCl}_2$ and $\text{BaCl}_2$ are all ionic and already dissolved, so we just compare their hydroxides. $\text{NaOH}$ is very soluble and $\text{Ba}(\text{OH})_2$ is soluble enough that no precipitate forms under these conditions.

$$\text{Mg}^{2+} + 2\text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{Mg}(\text{OH})_2(s)$$

Only magnesium gives the familiar white precipitate of $\text{Mg}(\text{OH})_2$.

**Test the covalent chloride**

$\text{SiCl}_4(\text{l})$ is completely different. It is covalent and hydrolyses vigorously in water, even without alkali:

$$\text{SiCl}_4 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{SiO}_2(s) + 4\text{HCl}$$

$\text{SiO}_2$, hydrated silica, appears as a white solid. The $\text{NH}_3$ just neutralises the $\text{HCl}$ formed, driving the reaction on. So the two white precipitates are from $\text{MgCl}_2$ and $\text{SiCl}_4$.

options.A: MgCl2 is correct because white Mg(OH)2 precipitates, but BaCl2 is wrong. Ba(OH)2 is soluble (Group 2 hydroxides become more soluble down the group), so no precipitate forms with NH3(aq).
options.B: This is correct. Mg2+ gives white insoluble Mg(OH)2 with the OH- from ammonia, and SiCl4 hydrolyses to give white solid SiO2 (silica). These are the only two precipitates.
options.C: Both are wrong. NaOH is very soluble so NaCl gives no precipitate, and Ba(OH)2 is also soluble enough to stay in solution, so BaCl2 gives no precipitate.
options.D: SiCl4 is correct because it hydrolyses to white SiO2, but NaCl is wrong. Sodium salts and sodium hydroxide are all soluble, so NH3(aq) causes no change with NaCl(aq).
